claim: How we end our night has a huge impact on the next day, undeniably seen personally and "over and over and over and over again with nearly every coaching client", in some way or another
name: Evening routine

claim: The next day actually starts the night before: tonight's wrap-up is going to actually determine how tomorrow starts, which might be emotionally, energetically, when you get up, what you do or don't do
name: Evening routine

claim: How we end our night "is a little lever" that opens or closes big doors
name: Evening routine

claim: Seen with so many guys: an early evening going a certain way gets them off track and they use porn later at night, or maybe get distracted by the internet or otherwise off track and stay up super late, later than they should, want or intend, affecting the next day
name: Evening routine

claim: Examples are limitless of how the night affects the next day, but "truly tomorrow starts tonight"
name: Evening routine

claim: A lot of how your night affects the next day is very unique to you, so with intention and awareness, debrief your nights: what at night often leads to what the next day
name: Evening routine

claim: When a morning goes really well (feeling great, maybe hormones in a great place, good morning wood, strong, disciplined, up early, workout done), ask how last night led to that
name: Evening routine

claim: When you get off track, debrief how the night before led to that too
name: Evening routine

claim: Pay attention to the little levers in your night; they vary a ton
name: Evening routine

claim: One example seen of a little lever in the night: taking five minutes between work and home to be really intentional, maybe meditating five minutes or setting intentions for the night, can have a huge impact, one way or the other
name: Evening routine

claim: Coming up often personally, and heard from clients: an underlying angst, as the day wears on, that not enough happened or got done today, or maybe about big-picture things you want to change that haven't changed yet
name: Evening routine

claim: Open loops: our mind does not like open loops and wants to close them
name: Evening routine

claim: Promising to tell someone something later opens a loop in their mind; never addressed, the open loop creates a little uneasiness, depending on interest
name: Evening routine

claim: Your mind opens loops with your own life: planning tomorrow opens a bunch of loops, and the day probably opens a bunch more
name: Evening routine

claim: It seems open loops often affect us at the end of the day as uneasiness, one way being trouble getting to sleep, kept up by something underlying you're not conscious of
name: Evening routine

claim: It seems the angst over open loops keeps us from being willing to actually end the day
name: Evening routine

claim: Tool one for ending the night, a snapshot recap, usable anytime: at the end of a workday before home life, or in bed at night, "a great time to do it"
name: Evening routine

claim: For a snapshot recap, for 30 seconds to a couple of minutes, close your eyes and let snapshots of the day flow through your mind from start to finish, up to that moment, without thinking about it, judging it or feeling bad
name: Evening routine

claim: In a snapshot recap of the day, maybe just five, 10, 15 snapshots: little video clips or, if you're not visual, a sort of awareness
name: Evening routine

claim: Even if things you wanted didn't get done, recalling how the day went in a snapshot recap "really tends to close a lot of those open loops": you may fall asleep easier or, done earlier in the evening, move on more easily with your night
name: Evening routine

claim: Experiment with when to do the snapshot recap of the day; at a minimum, a suggestion: try it when you get in bed
name: Evening routine

claim: In the snapshot recap of the day, no judgment, neither bad about what got done nor really great about what went great: just pass through as an observer
name: Evening routine

claim: Tool two for ending the night, very simple but "very, very powerful": be willing to acknowledge "today's over, today was enough, I'm enough", let go of the day and start again tomorrow
name: Evening routine

claim: For a very long time, acknowledging "today's over, today was enough, I'm enough" was not a tool in the mental toolbox
name: Evening routine

claim: Often, in an underlying way, we don't acknowledge that today's over and was enough: a background program says I didn't get this or that done, I'm not enough because this thing hasn't changed
name: Being enough

claim: Take 10 seconds, at some point or maybe multiple points in the evening, maybe even verbally, at least in your mind and heart: today's done, it was enough, I'm enough, letting it go, moving on
name: Evening routine

claim: The acknowledgment "today's over, today was enough, I'm enough" "very well may make the difference" in going to bed on time, falling asleep, doing a meditation at the end of the night [?], or ending the night more disciplined, grounded and centered
name: Evening routine

claim: Heard from a lot of clients, and definitely felt personally: not acknowledging that today's over and was enough can often lead to staying up much later than we should, from an unconscious hesitation to let go of the day while other things might still get done
name: Evening routine

claim: Of the two tools for ending the night, the snapshot recap and the acknowledgment that today was enough, the acknowledgment is used more regularly personally and probably depended on more, maybe even more important
name: Evening routine

claim: The "I'm enough" part of the acknowledgment at the end of the day matters: probably no one ever met personally has the knowing, "a hundred percent in every cell of their body", that they're enough; we have little layers of thinking we're not good enough
name: Being enough

claim: The 10 seconds of acknowledging that today was enough and you're enough are huge, "a game changer", so simple; it seems you might be surprised at how impactful that can be
name: Evening routine
